en: The Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī of the Supreme Buddha for the General and Great Commander Aṭavaka:
The Ritual Manual for Practice, Scroll One;
also known as the All-Body Vajra-Samaya.
The One Named Infinite Nectar Supernatural Power, translated by the Great Master Amoghavajra at the Inner Altar of the Buddhist Way. Thus have I heard.
At one time, the Buddha was staying between the twin śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus,
as well as thirty-six thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
among whom were the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and others.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva,
and Amoghapāśa Bodhisattva.
Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa,
Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara,
and Bodhisattva Samādhy-aiśvarya-rāja were their leaders.
Furthermore, there were bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās;
as well as devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings, the four world-protecting heavenly kings, vajrapāṇis, and spirits.
Asuras, gandharva kings, kinnaras, mahoragas,
yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, apasmāras, kūṣmāṇḍas, piśācas, and the mātṛkā-gaṇas.
Together with their retinues and women, they paid respectful homage and made offerings;
filled with joy, they sat surrounding him to listen to the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly, saying:
"Now that the Four Great Elements are about to sink into parinirvāṇa," the fourfold assembly heard this and wailed and wept aloud:
"Alas! Why do you intend to abandon us, the great multitude, and enter nirvāṇa?"
The world is empty and the Māra-king is rampant;
we, this great assembly, have no place of refuge.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will remain further in this world.
He subdued the Māra King, causing him to resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment,
and delivered us— the fourfold assembly— safely into nirvāṇa.
The Buddha then addressed the good sons and good daughters:
The time for my parinirvāṇa is now approaching;
I shall not remain long in this world.
You should not weep.
I now entrust all my disciples to you, O Bodhisattvas;
together you shall instruct and deliver them.
Even were I to remain in the world further, [it would be no different].
All sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm utterly loathe and despise me;
for long kalpas, the Māra-king and the six heretical teachers have harbored resentment toward me without ceasing.
The sentient beings within the assembly inform one another of this.
"While the World-Honored One was in the world, we, the great assembly, took refuge in him as our place of reliance;
he liberated us from our afflictions.
Now that the unsurpassed World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa,"
"Our retinue will surely be beset by the King of Māras.
Having thus informed one another, they shed tears like rain;
wailing with their whole bodies, they fainted and fell to the ground, blood flowing from their mouths.
The various devas caused Mount Sumeru, the mountain of jewels, to tremble and shatter into particles as fine as dust.
All insects, beasts, and sentient beings with moving life simultaneously raised their voices in unison, crying out, "Alas, what suffering!"
"The Unsurpassed World-Honored One has abandoned us, the sentient beings of this turbid and evil kalpa who undergo great suffering and affliction.
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the fourfold assembly,
rose with composure and sat down cross-legged.
Tranquil and unmoving, he emitted a great radiance that reached upward to the Heaven of the Thirty-three and downward to the sentient beings in the eighteen hells.
The heavens and earth shook in six ways, and *mandārava* flowers rained down.
They completely covered the great earth of the trichiliocosm.
Celestial drums resounded spontaneously and banners and streamers rose up of their own accord.
With joy, they joined their palms toward the Buddha and listened to the Dharma with single-minded devotion.
The Buddha addressed the entire assembly, saying:
"At present, the sentient beings of this country are undergoing various sufferings and afflictions.
There is an elder named Licchavi."
They are deluded and disturbed by various malevolent spirits;
they howl, run about, and harass their households without any place of refuge to report it.
Now, seeing this, they cry out in a loud voice:
"Homage to the Buddha! Homage to the Dharma! Homage to the Saṃgha! May you know this suffering of mine.
The Buddha then commanded Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Take the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa mantra and go to rescue the Licchavis, so that they may attain liberation."
At that time, Maudgalyāyana, receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, vanished from the Śāla grove and appeared within the householder’s home.
He then addressed them, saying: "All you māras, spirits, and demons, listen attentively!"
The Unsurpassed Śākyamuni Buddha has charged me to uphold this Great Radiant Uṣṇīṣa Divine Mantra to subdue you,
hosts of Māras, and to protect the elder.
Thereupon, those ghosts and spirits retreated and fled;
they then entered the Śītavana forest to harass and disturb the Venerable Ānanda, preventing him from proceeding further.
At that time, various demons, ghosts, and spirits...
Knowing that Māra had arisen to cause disturbances because the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, Ānanda was present at the time.
There was a great general named Aṭavaka, who served as the commander-in-chief;
his heart was filled with wrath, and he immediately summoned the eight classes of spirits, including devas, nāgas, and asuras.
The Four Great Heavenly Kings, the twenty-eight yakṣa generals,
and the forty-two rākṣasa kings,
headed by Pūrṇabhadra.
He also summoned the various Vajra-ghana Guhyapatis, heroic warriors,
the King of Lion’s Roar, the King Mucilinda,
and all the celestial deities of great merit and eloquence.
The Peacock King, the Golden-Winged Bird King, and the Conqueror-of-Enemies Bird King,
together with all the devas, asuras, humans, non-humans, and others as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
were all fully armored; they shook heaven and moved the earth.
The four seas surge and boil; the Great Iron Ring Mountains, Mount Mucilinda, and the sevenfold mountains of precious jewels roar and split asunder.
Winds and clouds gather in ominous masses, thunderbolts crash down, and the light of the sun fades away.
The various devas and Brahmā kings find no peace in their palaces;
all sentient beings have lost the radiance of their countenances;
and dragons, snakes, tortoises, and turtles emerge from their burrows.
The ghosts, spirits, and māras shrieked and fled, crying out with one voice, "How great is this suffering! Alas, what agony!
In their frantic terror, they ran about, not knowing where to go.
The assembly all exclaimed in astonishment, "How strange!
What evil omen is this that we witness?
It causes our fourfold assembly to behold such fierce majesty."
He immediately rose, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One, for what reason do you manifest this sign,
causing all the ghosts, spirits, and asuras to find no peace in their abodes?"
"May the Buddha, out of compassion, take pity on and protect us.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly:
"I now wish to enter parinirvāṇa."
I entrust these Dharma-treasuries to you for their protection.
Now, all the ghosts, spirits, asuras, and virtuous deities who guard and protect the Dharma in the four directions— [may you likewise do so].
The General who Protects the World, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
the Vajrapāṇi, the Prajñā-benevolent deity;
and the eight classes of devas, nāgas, humans, and non-humans.
"Come all together to this assembly and bind yourselves by oath:
with one mind, protect the treasury of the Buddha's Dharma as well as you sentient beings,
so that there may be no decline or affliction."
From this day forward, may there be constant peace by day and night.
At that time, the Generalissimo and Great Commander summoned the King-Spirits of the four quarters to assemble at the Buddha’s dwelling;
each of them brought ointments, powdered incense, celestial garments, and jeweled necklaces.
Having circumambulated the Buddha a hundred thousand times, they prostrated at his feet and stood to one side.
With one voice, they addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we have heard that the World-Honored One intends to enter parinirvāṇa."
Sentient beings cherish him with a love like that of a child for its mother, never for a moment wishing to let him go;
the divine kings and others feel their hearts and livers torn to pieces,
praying only that the World-Honored One would remain in the world longer.
"Deliver all sentient beings, as well as ourselves, and lead us peacefully into nirvana.
At that time, Aṭavaka spoke these verses to the countless great deities:
We, the gods among gods, look with compassion upon all devas,
nāgas, asuras, and the assembly of the eight classes of spirits;
we regard them as our parents, never for a moment abandoning them from our hearts.
Suddenly proclaiming that you have entered nirvana,
our great host of deities has had its hearts and livers torn apart inch by inch.
We pray only for your great compassion, out of pity for all sentient beings.
"Having delivered my great assembly, how could I enter nirvāṇa?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly, saying:
"You great generals and mighty warriors, listen attentively; I shall speak for you."
The Dharma of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is like the mandārava flower, appearing only once in a long time;
when sentient beings see it, their hearts can never be satiated.
If I were to remain long in this world...
Being at enmity with Māra, sentient beings will despise and revile you,
causing those beings to sink into the ocean of suffering.
You, O General, are the foremost among all the deities.
Possessing extraordinary and inconceivable majestic power, you shall be protected by the Tathāgata;
after my parinirvāṇa, you shall guard the treasury of the Dharma as well as sentient beings,
causing them to be freed from suffering and hardship.
At that time, the Great General Aṭavaka,
together with the King of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, the spirit Vajrapāṇi, and Dhṛtarāṣṭra as their leaders,
addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we who are here now..."
With a single-minded vow, they bind the Great Vajra;
this is for the purpose of subduing all fierce and evil spirits and ghosts,
and for the purpose of causing all enemies, wicked people, and malevolent thieves to be brought under control.
It is because he wishes to protect all kings and ensure the peace and happiness of their people;
because he wishes to cause sentient beings to revere and honor the Triple Gem;
and because he wishes to cause the externalists, Māra Pāpīyān, and others to give rise to the bodhicitta.
"Because I wish to cause sentient beings to be free from the affliction of illness in their bodies,
and because I wish to prevent any spirit from opposing sentient beings,
World-Honored One, I now desire to lead before the Buddha an army of hundreds of billions of *Gaṅgā*-river-sands of powerful *yakṣa* spirit-kings."
With one mind, we shall protect and shield all sentient beings so that they may be freed from all demonic bonds.
World-Honored One, within this great assembly,
I shall bind a great divine mantra named the Amṛta-ananta-dhāraṇī.
It is for the purpose of subduing non-Buddhist heretics, evil ghosts and spirits, as well as wicked kings and evil ministers;
and to turn back those in the six realms of existence to guide and attract sentient beings, ensuring that none are harmed.
The Buddha addressed the Generalissimo Aṭavaka:
"I know that sentient beings are weak and inferior, and thus unable to uphold your boundless divine mantra.
I fear that in future generations they might cause harm to all living beings."
At that time, the celestial kings of the four quarters, Brahmā, and Śakra, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, this mantra is extremely fierce and of a most evil nature; it will surely cause harm.
At that time, Aṭavaka, with the kings Nanda, Bhīma, and Balāhaka, [spoke].
Everyone said, "The World-Honored One and all Buddhas draw in and gather sentient beings through the power of great compassion;
yet Ānanda has still been deluded by a Caṇḍāla woman."
The World-Honored One, the Yakṣa King Arida, dwells on Cold Mountain.
Leading ninety thousand followers, he daily devours immeasurable and boundless sentient beings;
all the Vajrapāṇi spirits and celestial armies are unable to subdue him.
The World-Honored One manifested through expedient transformation as the Generalissimo.
Thus, he conjured a powerful and majestic spirit who shook his palace with his body.
At that time, the mouth of the King of Ghosts bled, and he fell to the ground in a swoon.
Knowing that death would not be long in coming, he finally released him.
How could the World-Honored One have known that the body of this great general possessed such incomparable majesty and virtue?
World-Honored One, had I wished to practice the conduct of a bodhisattva and draw others in through compassion, [I would have done so].
If the ghost-king rākṣasa intends to cause harm and destroy sentient beings,
I may manifest as the Vajra King Hayagrīva,
and the sentient beings will immediately be struck with fear.
Or, when I acted as the Great Light Malla,
the asuras found no peace in their palaces.
World-Honored One, for this reason, I have become the Generalissimo and Great Commander of the ghosts and spirits.
Thus, sentient beings will delight in beholding him.
World-Honored One, I fear that after the parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One, during the hundred kalpas thereafter,
the Buddha-dharma will gradually perish and bodhisattvas will no longer see it.
The Vajra follows the place of bliss and purity.
When sentient beings have meager merit, demonic influences flourish;
the king lacks majesty and virtue, and the princes, ministers, and subjects find no happiness.
They harass sentient beings, sometimes absorbing their vital essence,
devouring their flesh and blood,
or causing them to die prematurely while still in the mother’s womb.
At this time, I am able to remain day and night without separation,
protecting and sustaining all sentient beings in birth and death so that they may leave behind their drowning in affliction.
World-Honored One, my body manifests an evil appearance, yet my mind gives rise to great compassion.
It is no different from how that king supports his people.
Wherever a son of the Buddha may be— whether in a stūpa,
in a temple, in the mountains, along a road, or in the wilderness— [he is supported].
"I vow to have compassion for them, to protect them, and not allow them to encounter evil.
World-Honored One, knowing our resolve, please accept this divine mantra from us.
The Buddha said, "So be it; for the sake of the thousand kalpas to come."
"You shall protect my inconceivable great treasury of the Dharma and shall skillfully expound this divine mantra for the sake of all sentient beings in future generations.

And their children, retinues, servants, and all minor poisonous and malevolent nāga sons—
whether manifesting through transformation as male forms, female forms, or the forms of birds, beasts, nāgas, or snakes.
Some have form and some are formless; some have heads and some are headless.
Some have feet and some are footless; some speak and some do not.
Yet those who come to engage in speech all walk backward and stop facing forward.
There may be the sun, moon, and stars in the sky—such as the Southern Dipper, the Northern Dipper, and malevolent stars—exhibiting strange and ominous transformations;
or there may be ghosts, spirits, rākṣasas, and yakṣas flying through the void.
Or they may produce thunder, lightning, and crashing bolts,
or release whirlwinds, solar discs, and lunar discs, all of which shall be extinguished.
All those who come to harass people shall likewise be destroyed.
Furthermore, the sentient beings of the world possess forms according to their respective categories:
whether they be grasses, trees, tiles, stones, flowers, fruits, food and drink,
clothing, birds, beasts, or the five elements.
Those who are able to cause transformations, terrors, exhaustion, and affliction for others shall all be eliminated and extinguished.
World-Honored One, if there are sentient beings who harbor mutual hatred and inflict harm upon one another—
whether taking human form or the forms of all manner of worldly objects— [they shall likewise be subdued].
Or they invoke mountain deities, tree deities, spirits of tombs, spirits of altars and fields, the sun and moon, and the stars;
or they perform sacrifices and recite incantations to the wind deities, fire deities, and the deities of water and earth,
concerning what has been done or not yet done, what has been accomplished or not yet accomplished, and what has been harmed or not yet harmed.
Should there be those who hear this great divine mantra of boundless ambrosia,
it shall cause those spirits, ghosts,
and those who perform [malevolent acts] to vanish and perish of their own accord, leaving nothing behind.
Blessed One, if there is a fever caused by a bhūtanaka,
or caused by an apasmāra, or caused by a ṭakkiṇī.
Whether it be for one day, two days, three days,
or four days; or for one month, half a month, one year, or half a year—
one who hears this divine mantra shall immediately attain its eradication.
There may be sentient beings who, in their previous lives, failed to revere the Triple Gem and disparaged the treasury of the Dharma;
consequently, when they obtain a human body, their various faculties are incomplete,
and their bodies are afflicted by all manner of evil diseases, such as malignant sores, scabs, and ringworms.
Or they may be afflicted by the disease of kāmalā;
such sentient beings are deeply pitiable.
World-Honored One, I wish to cause those sentient beings [to be freed from it].
Morning and evening, they give rise to the aspiration for the unsurpassed Way;
they repent and reproach themselves for the karma of their past lives;
and they cherish all beings with compassion, not begrudging even their own bodies or lives.
With a mind free from harm, cause the Three Jewels to bestow their empowerment,
so that the transgressions of the three karmas are eliminated and the six sense faculties are purified.
Thereafter, at dawn, recite this mantra one hundred and eight times.
By bathing the body and mind with consecrated water, one shall attain recovery within ten days. The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is. What you have said is indeed no different from the truth."
This mantra possesses such benefits.
All you great assemblies of spirits and deities, listen each with a single mind as I speak:
among the eight classes of beings, there is a Commander-in-Chief and Great General whose name is Āṭavaka.
Having constantly made offerings to boundless Buddhas, you now draw near to Śākyamuni;
manifesting the body of a Bodhisattva of great compassion, you assume a terrifying form through which all ghosts and spirits submit,
and the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa do likewise.
Able to extract them from suffering and affliction within the six realms, causing all to attain happiness;
if there are sentient beings who hear their name, they will forever be free from calamities and perils.
At the time of death, they shall have no fear or dread, for the Bodhisattvas shall bestow upon them bodhi.
If there be any who oppose this mantra, their present bodies shall be afflicted with white leprosy and flow with pus and blood;
thereafter they shall fall into hell and undergo all manner of suffering. Even if they later become human again, they shall be incomplete in their faculties.
I now summon them to serve as my generals, titled "The Boundless Mantra of Ambrosia."
If there are sentient beings who skillfully receive and uphold [this], all Buddhas shall bear witness to it.
At that time, Aṭavaka addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I am the witness for all the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of spirits, ghosts, and asuras."
Among humans and non-humans alike, they serve as generals and great commanders who command ghosts and spirits to protect the lands and sustain sentient beings—
all this is achieved by upholding my divine mantra.
Thus, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the final five hundred years, the kalpa-turbidity will arise;
spirits and demons will flourish while the merit of sentient beings becomes thin,
and they will be afflicted by various ghosts and māras.
Those who drink vital essence or devour flesh and blood cause pestilence and fever in people,
whether for one day, two days, three days, or four days.
For up to seven days, half a month, or a full month,
all afflictions such as headaches, earaches, backaches, heartaches, pains in the hands, pains in the feet,
and pains in all the limbs and joints shall be completely eliminated.
All such spirits— whether devas,
nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, rākṣasas, bhūtas, or kaṭapūtanas— [are likewise].
Non-Buddhists, celestial Māras, those wandering through the six realms,
ghosts, and spirits; or evil persons, wicked bandits, tigers, wolves, lions, centipedes, pythons, and snakes—
such beings who inflict harm upon humans.
By the power of this divine mantra, one is able to restrain, bind, and utterly destroy evil spirits and ghosts;
it causes the great powerful warriors to lift up a thousand-spoked wheel with their palms and crush their heads,
shattering them into seven pieces.
Even if one’s body were analyzed into atoms and one’s prohibitions broken so as to lose one’s life,
one could not cause harm to the land or to sentient beings.
World-Honored One, I shall now further recite a divine mantra.
He caused those who receive and uphold [this teaching] to perform the ritual of boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*).
Aṭavaka then spoke this mantra for binding the boundary:
Oṃ lekha lekha sara sara sara sara phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā. He further spoke the general mantra of the eight classes of spirits:
Namo buddhāya | Namo dharmāya | Namo saṃghāya | Namo bhṛkuṭīkṣaṇāya | Namo tiṣyabhrūkuṭīkṣaṇāya | Namo... (The text provided ends here).
Ka-la-ya-kṣa-ha-ha-ha-ha-ha-ha-ha-ha-hu-hu-hu-hu-hu-hu-hu-hu-he-he-he-he-he-he-he-he-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-pu.
Puṇya puṇya puṇya puṇya puṇya | Nīra nīra nīra nīra nīra nīra | Kṣetra kṣetra kṣetra kṣetra kṣetra kṣetra | Bala bala bala bala bala bala | Loka loka loka loka loka loka.
Imperative command! Imperative command! Imperative command! Imperative command! Imperative command! Imperative command! Imperative command! Haste! Haste! Haste! Haste! Haste! Haste! Haste!
*Vāṃ vāṃ vāṃ vāṃ vāṃ vāṃ vāṃ* | *Aṭa bha ku ya hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. If one wishes to summon the deities of the eight classes:
If one binds the mudrās of the eight classes and recites their mantras twenty-one times, their deities will arrive immediately.
The boundary established by the World-Honored One extends for a thousand yojanas on each side, serving as a protective perimeter.
First, recite the mantra over pure water and scatter it in the four directions.
Next, recite the mantra over pure ash and scatter it in the four directions.
Finally, recite the mantra over powdered incense and pure earth and scatter them in the four directions.

One then recites mantras over white mustard seeds and scatters them in the four directions—according to one version, at this point one may either recite mantras over swords or recite mantras over lumps of clay and throw them in the four directions, or recite mantras over bows and arrows and shoot them in the four directions; wherever they reach according to the extent of their power shall constitute the boundary.
There were all spirits, ghosts, devas, nāgas, and asuras;
the Four Heavenly Kings each led twenty-eight divisions of great yakṣa generals, forty-two divisions of rākṣasa armies, nāga kings, and kumbhāṇḍa kings.
With one mind, they shall protect [the practitioner], never departing day or night to guard and sustain this person.
When the World-Honored One wishes to establish the boundary,
[the practitioner] shall bathe in pure scented water and don exquisite, superior garments.
One shall not consume the five pungent herbs, wine, meat, or their like;
nor shall turnip, radish, daikon, or chives and onions pass through the mouth, maintaining purity and cleanliness.
World-Honored One, this mantra is peerlessly extraordinary, majestic, and sovereign.
Just as my own body is indestructible like a vajra,
all devas, humans, arhats, and the four world-protecting heavenly kings will give rise to joy and protect that person.
"Are you not aware, World-Honored One, that I am able to act as a Buddha in this world of five turbidities to rescue and protect sentient beings?
To extract the arrows of the three poisons, to turn them back from the six realms of existence,
and to guide and draw them forth so they may escape?"
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is.
The World-Honored One has commanded me to serve as the Generalissimo to protect and uphold the treasury of the Dharma.
Since beginningless time, my majestic power has been extraordinary, and my rank is equal to that of the Ten Stages."

I shall now further explain for the mantra-practitioner the protection-body mantra; this mantra will be explained later. When it has been recited seven full times, one should burn incense, sprinkle water upon the ground, and invoke all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, Devas, and others of the past, present, and future.
First, recite this mantra twenty-one times to bind the realm of space.
Next, recite the Mañjuśrī-mūla-kalpa-mantra to bind the boundary.
Then, recite the mantra of the Four Heavenly Kings to bind the celestial realm.
Next, recite the Vajra-mantra to bind the great boundary in the air.
Request the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) of the world to serve as the presiding master of the altar.
Next, request King Śama to serve as the guardian of the altar.
Next, he summoned the karmadeva rākṣasas to assist at the altar.
Once the invocation of the deities was complete,
he immediately requested Vairocana Buddha and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to serve as his preceptors.
I request Mañjuśrī to bear witness as I address the Earth Goddess Sthāvarā:
"O Great King of All Auspicious Deities, I wish to excavate a mandala site upon this ground."
To fulfill his wish,
he immediately burned incense, prepared food offerings, and made worship for one night.
On the following day, before the sun had risen, [he proceeded].
Take one *dō* of well-water from the morning dew and divide it into four vessels placed at the four cardinal directions.
Upon the water, place a sword, a bow, and arrows.
Then, dig three feet deep; you shall see the object.
If one sees a human being,
that person’s power of incantations can topple mountains and dry up the oceans;
if one sees insects or beasts, [the same applies].
The power of that person’s incantation is also like obtaining jade;
such a person is one who was present at the first assembly.
If one obtains gold or silver,
that person will become immensely wealthy by virtue of the mantra;
if one obtains items such as swords, weapons, bows, or arrows, [the same shall apply].
Within the altar, that person sees the deity of the mantra.
If they obtain the medicine,
that person will be well able to eliminate their illness.
If one obtains iron or stone,
that person will ultimately never regress and will attain firm, unimpeded wisdom.
Once these signs have been obtained, one should immediately receive the precepts of fasting.
From a separate location, take pure earth and dig out three feet of impure soil.
Separately collect the pure earth, sift and pound it, mix it with powdered incense, and compact it.
Leave a space of one chi above the ground in three layers.
The lower part is square and the upper part is circular, opened with twelve gateways.
It measures four cubits in length and breadth; its four sides are colored with five-colored clay, while the lower terrace is smeared with white earth mixed with fragrant water.
Above, smear it with cow dung mixed with incense.
Upon the altar, and at its center, place the śarīra within a vessel of white crystal, containing various types of incense.
Bodhisattva seats are arranged on the four sides of the Śāri [stūpa].
On the central altar base, twenty-four ritual water jars (kalaśa) are placed,
all filled with scented water, lotus flowers, and willow branches.
In the northeast corner, place a blue lotus seat to await me.
In the east, place the seat of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
In the southeast corner, place the seat of Kumbhīra.
In the south, place the seat of Virūḍhaka;
in the southwest, place the seat of Virūpākṣa;
in the west, place the seat of Virūḍhaka.
In the northwest, place the seat of the Great Blue-Faced One;
in the north, place the seat of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.
Around the base of the altar, seats are placed all around.
In total, there were forty-nine structures and forty-nine trays.
One hundred blades stood upright, all as sharp as frost;
at the topmost foundation, forty-two blades stood upright.
Twenty-four knives for the middle foundation;
thirty-six knives for the lower foundation;
twenty-eight knives and one hundred arrows placed around the altar below the foundation.
The upper foundation consists of twelve slabs;
the western side forms the entrance.
The middle foundation consists of twenty slabs.
On the outer edge of the lower base, four water basins are installed;
within these basins are flowers.
On the upper base, four vajras are installed.
On the lower base, place spears and swords;
on the middle base, place wheels;
outside the altar, place twelve clubs and eight iron staffs.
Place ten *kundikā* water-pots with cypress leaves in them;
make the food trays from lotus leaves.
Install an earthen fire-pit in the southwest corner of the altar.
The center is high and the four sides are low;
burn *sugandha*, honey, and wax.
Upon the upper base, place a single incense burner.
Place four relics of the Buddha upon the altar.
The mantra-practitioner sits facing east on a couch-grass mat;
kneeling with hands joined in prayer and holding an incense burner, he performs the invocation.
Then, having bound the boundary and formed the *mālā-mudrā* (flower-garland seal) with palms facing upward,
and after the seat has been stabilized, once again bind the boundary;
then burn incense, scatter flowers, and offer food.
Next, in the hearth to the southwest of this [altar], burn sesame seeds, non-glutinous rice, honey, curd, and ghee;
having finished burning various kinds of food and drink, say:
"May all the assemblies of noble ones, possessing a sense of shame and remorse, descend to this place."
One should immediately recite the Great Dharani one hundred and eight times,
holding a ritual mallet (vajra) and stamping the ground while reciting it.
Alternatively, if one holds a bow and arrows, the ghosts and spirits will arrive immediately.
Regarding this rite, the fifteenth day of the first month is considered the most auspicious.
On the seventh day of any other month, one may enter the maṇḍala.
With a sincere heart and focused mind, do not allow any distraction to arise.
On that very night, a young boy appeared.
On the third night, sixteen princes appeared.
On the fifth day, a great wind arose and dust swirled up.
On the night of the sixth day, it rained while we sat in meditation.
On the night of the seventh day, I, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, my mother,
and the Buddhas and spirits of the ten directions all entered the ritual altar.
A brilliant light shone forth;
upon the altar, bows and swords rang out spontaneously, and water jars turned of their own accord.
When I manifest my form during the latter part of the night, [you shall see me].
All ghosts and spirits will likewise manifest.
When performing the rite of boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*),
do not allow children or women to enter within.
If the boundary is established for seven days, it will only then be perfected.
Once the boundary is established, no malevolent spirits or ghosts shall enter within to cause disturbance,
whether they be those who oppose the devas or those who oppose the gandharvas.
Whether it be that which is contravened by asuras, or that which is contravened by kinnaras and garuḍas,
or that which is contravened by rākṣasas,
or that which is contravened by wind deities and fire deities.
All shall have their heads shattered and crushed, losing their mindfulness;
I shall crush those spirits with my thousand-spoked wheel to bring about their ruin and harm.
Should any evil thieves enter our realm, [they shall likewise suffer].
The Ghost King who Protects the Boundary dismembers and utterly destroys [the offender].
If one violates the upper altar,
the Great Malla Vajra raises a fire that burns them until they become red and swollen.
He will recover within three days.
If a person does not act according to this method, they will suffer calamity and misfortune.
On the seventh day, enter the *maṇḍala*.
Once defecate and once bathe;
change clothes at the three periods of the day;
enter the altar for six periods and perform the Way (practice) for six periods throughout one day and night, prostrating seven times.
Once a day at dawn, one should perform a single delimitation of the boundary (*sīmābandha*).
Before the ritual fast (*upavāsa*), one should dissolve the boundary; at night before sleeping, one should establish a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) to protect the body.
Forty-nine recitations for a single session is considered the medium standard.
One hundred and eight recitations are considered superior;
twenty-one recitations are considered inferior.
By doing so for one day and one night, one will be able to protect one's own body.
On the second day, one is able to protect one's household;
from the third day onward, one is able to protect others, bind ghosts and spirits,
and achieve all that is spoken.
When the seven days are complete, all the celestial kings, asura kings, naga kings, the spirit Generalissimo (Samantabhadra), and the vajra-wielding heroes will constantly remain at his side.
Even if [the rite] is not completed within those seven days, [they shall protect him].
After seven days, fourteen days, or twenty-one days,
and continuing up to forty-nine days, it will certainly succeed.
If one wishes to become a powerful mantra-practitioner, [one should do so].
Do not give rise to envy or malice in your mind.
Do not harbor pride toward any sentient beings, and do not speak of the mantras or the body of the deity.
Without passing even a hundred days, you will surely achieve accomplishment.
Possessing great power and fully endowed with boundless merit,
you are preeminent in the foremost rank and have attained the tenth bhūmi.
World-Honored One, I now act as a constant protector for those who maintain this recitation.
And he spoke the mantra, saying:

Oṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā | Sañji-ka phaṭ | Mahā-sañji-ka phaṭ | Mahā-ni-bha-tra phaṭ | Mahā-ra-tra phaṭ | Yakṣa phaṭ | Mahā-yakṣa phaṭ | Yakṣa phaṭ | Yakṣa phaṭ | Phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ | Ye hūṃ kha hūṃ kha | Urgently! Ye svāhā! "World-Honored One, this mantra possesses supreme great spiritual power and supreme majestic virtue."
It can cause the trichiliocosm to shake in six ways;
it can cause the four oceans to dry up and boil over;
and it can shatter Mount Sumeru into atoms as fine as motes of dust.
All various activities, such as moving mountains and halting flowing streams,
are completely fulfilled.
If there are spirits, *vināyakas*, or others who create obstacles for people or cause ruin and harm, [they shall be subdued].
By means of this divine mantra, one hurls those spirits and ghosts into the void,
where they no longer descend and are unable to cause harm or affliction.
World-Honored One, this mantra universally provides protection and salvation for all sentient beings.
If there are malevolent spirits that suck the vital essence from people,
harm their assets, or deplete their wealth—
if such beings cause fear among all sentient beings, this shall serve as a boundary for them all.
May those evil spirits, wicked people, and malevolent thieves be naturally dissipated and extinguished;
as shall all birds, beasts, plants, trees, pebbles, and stones in the world that are capable of harboring poison and harming people.
It eradicates them without remainder.
World-Honored One, this mantra possesses supreme majestic power;
it is extraordinary, fierce, and peerlessly formidable.
The World-Honored One, the eight-armed deity Nārāyaṇa,
is able to cause the bodies of the thirty-three devas to enter within a mustard seed,
such that Śakra and Brahmā do not perceive it at all.
Such is his supernormal power.
World-Honored One, suppose those celestial deities were to fill the world like rice, hemp, bamboo, or reeds.
May each and every celestial deity unite their minds and join their strength;
by the power of this great and boundless divine mantra of mine,
may those celestial deities be cast away to other worlds.
I cause those celestial deities to be neither aware nor cognizant [of my presence].
Such is the power of my own majesty as the Boundless Sovereign Generalissimo.
If good men or good women, kings, or ministers should receive and uphold this mantra, [they shall likewise be protected].
I shall [be accompanied] by all the Vajrapāṇis,
the devas, nāgas, asura kings, the four great heavenly kings,
and the twenty-eight divisions of yakṣa generals.
The forty-two classes of rākṣasa yakṣa kings;
the rākṣasa kumbhāṇḍa kings, gandharva kings, kiṃnara kings;

the king of the *vainateya* birds, the king mucilinda, the peacock king, the garuḍa king, the lion-roaring king, the great brahmā king, the king of merit and great eloquence, the maheśvara king, the king of the thirty-three heavens, and all the benevolent deities.
Each leads ten billion ghost-king generals,
fully equipped with armor and surrounding them from front and rear,
attending upon that person to ensure they do not encounter evil.
"Bhagavān, I am the Generalissimo and Great Commander among the kings of the ghost spirits.
Possessing boundless and sovereign power,
I am able to subdue and conquer the heretics, devas, nāgas, asura kings, and Brahmā kings."
If there should be any who transgress,
I shall crush their heads with a thousand-spoked wheel until they are shattered like fine dust,
causing them to be utterly extinguished.
World-Honored One, if any devas, nāgas, or any kṣetrapāla spirits hear my name,
Aṭṭhapaku, they will rush forward to welcome me;
how much more so those who can further receive and uphold it according to the Dharma?
World-Honored One, those who hear the names of these divine mantras shall immediately pay respectful homage,
or else join their palms in praise.
Whoever has previously shared a profound and heavy karmic connection with the Buddha will, in this present life,
hear this dhāraṇī again with great intensity.
World-Honored One, if one is able to recite it, they shall not be harassed or afflicted by ghosts or spirits.
Furthermore, they shall not suffer from sudden illness nor die an untimely death;
they shall attain a lifespan of a hundred years and witness a hundred autumns, never encountering evil.
World-Honored One, if anyone practices this path of incantation...
Even if one does not become a great master of mantras,
one will still be able to accomplish various meritorious qualities,
attain an excellent official rank, and possess incomparable skill in debate.
There shall be no hardship from the shackles of royal law, nor any hardship from blades or clubs.
One shall be liberated from entanglements and fetters, illuminating the darkness,
and completely extinguishing all poisonous, evil bonds.
Even mad elephants, mad bandits, tigers, wolves,
and lions shall have their mouths closed and throats constricted so that they cannot harm people;
therefore, it is named the "Amṛta Dhāraṇī of the Great Treasury King, the Transformation General of Bodhisattva Akṣayamati."
World-Honored One, if there are sentient beings who possess no merit,
the Buddha Vairocana would certainly not have authorized me to seal this with his seal.
It is titled the "Dhāraṇī General of Boundless Nectar" (Ananta-amṛta-dhāraṇī-senāpati-mantra).
World-Honored One, for those who uphold this mantra,
there are ten great benefits and merits that accompany them.
First, by skillfully upholding the path of the mantra, they will surely attain the unsurpassed good path.
Second, they can transfer to their place of rebirth and go there at will.
Third, while living there, they are not startled, terrified, or harmed by weapons or warfare.
Fourth, they do not fear venomous insects or predatory beasts.
Fifth, one does not fear imprisonment by royal law;
sixth, one is not harmed by enemies;
seventh, there are no obstacles wherever one goes.
Eighth, all people believe and accept the teachings they utter.
Ninth, they experience neither hunger nor thirst.
Tenth, at the time of death, they do not encounter the eight difficulties.
Having beheld Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva face to face and received the prediction of enlightenment,
those who recite this mantra, O World-Honored One,
shall obtain immeasurable, extraordinary benefits and merit.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Samādhi-viśeṣa-rāja.
He adjusted his robes and bared his right shoulder.
Placing his right knee on the ground and joining his palms, he addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One, I see within this assembly the Generalissimo Aṭavaka,
who leads the eight classes of divine beings, including devas and nāgas."
Clad in armor and wielding spears, his radiance shines brilliantly and his majestic power is extraordinary.
Should he give rise to wrath, he causes all the ghosts and spirits to vanish and perish of their own accord,
and the heavens and earth tremble in six ways.
"Bhagavān, what samādhis and merits did this Great General practice in his previous lives, and what vows did he make,
that he now possesses such a body of great majestic power and extraordinary excellence?"
Now this mantra has been recited as above.
The fourfold assembly is struck with wonder, doubt, and amazement at its extraordinary nature.
We pray that the Buddha, out of his great compassion, will explain it for us; we wish to hear it.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva King of Sovereignty over Samādhi:
"Listen attentively now, as I shall speak of the past conduct of that Great General.
Good son, that Great General—"
He cultivated the bodhisattva practices in the presence of the Tathāgata King of Emptiness.
After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma,
sentient beings possessed meager merit and suffered from a three-year drought.
The land became crimson for a thousand li and the flowing waters dried up.
All sentient beings lost their original nature, and those suffering from hunger and thirst filled the roads.
At that time, that great general first became a lay practitioner (śrāmaṇera).
His family was very wealthy;
seeing those sentient beings undergoing such suffering,
he immediately abandoned his wife, children, and kinsmen.
Wearing old and tattered clothes, he carried water and food,
traveling everywhere to relieve people from hunger and thirst;
he practiced such deeds for sixty years without ceasing, applying himself with diligent effort.
He then encountered chaos and disorder, being surrounded, seized, and bound by a band of mad rebels who reviled him.
At that time, the practitioner, knowing himself to be innocent, spoke these words:
"I pray now that this band of rebels will release my hands and feet."
I prostrate to the ten directions and take refuge in the Triple Gem.
This year my life has reached its decline; I am old and shall soon die.
Upon hearing this, the bandits immediately released his hands and feet.
